danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 10
paragraphs: I pausen kom et pust af kold luft ind i Hélènes loge, døren gik op, og Anatol trådte ind, bøjende sig for ikke at støde imod nogen.
»Lad mig præsentere min bror for dig,« sagde Hélène, idet hendes øjne uroligt flakkede fra Natasja til Anatol.

Natasja drejede sit lille, smukke hoved mod den elegante, unge officer og smilede til ham over sin bare skulder. Anatol, der var lige så flot på nært hold som på afstand, satte sig ved siden af hende og fortalte, at han længe havde ønsket denne lykke — lige siden Narysjkin-ballet, hvor han havde haft den velkendte fornøjelse at se hende. Kuragin var langt mere forstandig og naturlig med kvinder end blandt mænd. Han talte dristigt og ukunstlet, og Natasja blev mærkeligt og behageligt overrasket over, at der ikke var noget skræmmende ved denne mand, der blev talt så meget om, men at hans smil tværtimod var yderst åbent, muntert og godhjertet.
Kuragin spurgte hende om hendes mening om forestillingen og fortalte hende, hvordan Semjonova ved en tidligere forestilling var faldet ned på scenen.

»Og ved De hvad, grevinde,« sagde han og tiltale hende pludselig, som om hun var en gammel, fortrolig bekendt, »vi arrangerer et kostume-turné; De burde deltage! Det bliver vældig morsomt. Vi skal alle mødes hos Karaginerne! Vær venlig at komme! Nej! Vil De virkelig, hvad?« sagde han.

Mens han sagde dette, fjernede han aldrig sine smilende øjne fra hendes ansigt, hendes hals og hendes bare arme. Natasja vidste med sikkerhed, at han var betaget af hende. Det behagede hende, og alligevel gjorde hans nærvær hende beklemt og trykket. Når hun ikke så på ham, følte hun, at han kiggede på hendes skuldre, og hun fangede ufrivilligt hans blik, så han hellere skulle se ind i hendes øjne. Men når hun kiggede ind i hans øjne, blev hun skræmt, idet hun indså, at der ikke var den barriere af blufærdighed, hun altid havde følt mellem sig selv og andre mænd. Hun vidste ikke, hvordan det var gået til, at hun inden for fem minutter var kommet til at føle sig forfærdelig tæt på denne mand. Når hun vendte sig bort, frygtede hun, at han bagfra kunne gribe hendes bare arm og kysse hende på halsen. De talte om de mest almindelige ting, og alligevel følte hun, at de var tættere på hinanden, end hun nogensinde havde været på nogen mand. Natasja vendte sig hele tiden mod Hélène og mod sin far, som for at spørge, hvad det hele betød, men Hélène var optaget af samtale med en general og svarede ikke på hendes blik, og hendes fars øjne sagde intet andet end hvad de altid sagde: »Morer du dig? Nå, det glæder mig!«

I et af disse øjeblikke af pinlig tavshed, da Anatols fremtrædende øjne roligt og fast stirrede på hende, spurgte Natasja ham, for at bryde tavsheden, hvordan han kunne lide Moskva. Hun stillede spørgsmålet og rødmede. Hun følte hele tiden, at hun ved at tale med ham gjorde noget upassende. Anatol smilede som for at opmuntre hende.

»I begyndelsen brød jeg mig ikke så meget om det, for det, der gør en by behagelig, ce sont les jolies femmes,* ikke sandt? Men nu kan jeg lide det rigtig godt,« sagde han og kiggede meningsfuldt på hende. »De kommer til kostume-turnéen, grevinde? Kom nu!« og idet han rakte hånden ud mod hendes buket og sænkede stemmen, tilføjede han: »De bliver den smukkeste der. Kom, kære grevinde, og giv mig denne blomst som et pant!«
* De smukke kvinder.

Natasja forstod ikke, hvad han sagde, lige så lidt som han selv, men hun følte, at hans uforståelige ord rummede en utilbørlig hensigt. Hun vidste ikke, hvad hun skulle sige, og vendte sig bort, som om hun ikke havde hørt hans bemærkning. Men så snart hun havde vendt sig bort, følte hun, at han var der, bagved, så tæt bag hende.

»Hvordan er han nu? Forvirret? Vred? Burde jeg rette det?« spurgte hun sig selv, og hun kunne ikke lade være med at vende sig om. Hun så lige ind i hans øjne, og hans nærhed, selvtillid og det godmodige smils ømhed besejrede hende. Hun smilede, ligesom han, og kiggede lige ind i hans øjne. Og igen følte hun med rædsel, at ingen barriere var imellem ham og hende.

Tæppet gik op igen. Anatol forlod logen, rolig og munter. Natasja gik tilbage til sin far i den anden loge, nu helt underkastet den verden, hun befandt sig i. Alt, der foregik foran hende nu, forekom helt naturligt, men til gengæld faldt alle hendes tidligere tanker om sin forlovede, om fyrstinde Marja eller om livet på landet hende ikke ind en eneste gang og var som tilhørende en fjern fortid.

I fjerde akt var der en slags djævel, der sang og viftede med armen, indtil brædderne blev trukket væk under ham, og han forsvandt ned under scenen. Det var den eneste del af fjerde akt, Natasja så. Hun følte sig oprørt og plaget, og årsagen var Kuragin, som hun ikke kunne lade være med at iagttage. Da de forlod teatret, kom Anatol hen til dem, tilkaldte deres vogn og hjalp dem ind. Mens han satte Natasja ind, trykkede han hendes arm over albuen. Ophidset og rød vendte hun sig om. Han kiggede på hende med glinsende øjne og smilede ømt.

Først da hun var nået hjem, var Natasja i stand til tydeligt at tænke over, hvad der var sket med hende, og idet hun pludselig huskede fyrst Andrej, blev hun forfærdet, og ved teen, som alle havde sat sig til efter operaen, udstødte hun et højt udbrud, rødmede og løb ud af stuen.

»Åh Gud! Jeg er fortabt!« sagde hun til sig selv. »Hvordan kunne jeg tillade det?« Hun sad længe med sit rødmende ansigt skjult i hænderne og forsøgte at fatte, hvad der var sket med hende, men var ude af stand til hverken at forstå, hvad der var sket, eller hvad hun følte. Alt syntes mørkt, uklart og forfærdeligt. Dér, i det enorme, oplyste teater, hvor den barberede Duport i en pailletsmykket jakke hoppede rundt til musikken på våde brædder, og unge piger og gamle mænd, og den næsten nøgne Hélène med sit stolte, rolige smil, henrykt råbte »bravo!« — dér, i Hélènes nærværelse, havde alt forekommet klart og enkelt; men nu, alene for sig selv, var det uforståeligt. »Hvad er det? Hvad var den rædsel, jeg følte for ham? Hvad er denne samvittighedsnag, jeg føler nu?« tænkte hun.

Kun for den gamle grevinde om natten i sengen kunne Natasja have fortalt alt, hvad hun følte. Hun vidste, at Sonja med sine strenge og enkle synspunkter enten slet ikke ville forstå det eller ville blive forfærdet over en sådan tilståelse. Så Natasja prøvede at løse det, der plagede hende, alene.

»Er jeg ødelagt for Andrejs kærlighed eller ej?« spurgte hun sig selv, og med beroligende ironi svarede hun: »Sikken en tåbe jeg er at spørge om det! Hvad skete der egentlig? Ingenting! Jeg har ikke gjort noget, jeg forledte ham ikke. Ingen får det at vide, og jeg ser ham aldrig igen,« sagde hun til sig selv. »Så det er klart, at der ikke er sket noget, og der er intet at fortryde, og Andrej kan stadig elske mig. Men hvorfor 'stadig'? Åh Gud, hvorfor er han ikke her?« Natasja beroligede sig for et øjeblik, men igen sagde et instinkt hende, at selvom alt dette var sandt, og selvom der ikke var sket noget, så var den tidligere renhed i hendes kærlighed til fyrst Andrej gået tabt. Og igen gennemgik hun i tankerne hele sin samtale med Kuragin og så igen ansigtet, gebærderne og det ømme smil hos den dristige, smukke mand, da han trykkede hendes arm.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: During the intermission, a whiff of cold air came into Helene's box, the door opened, and Anatole entered, stooping and trying not to brush against anyone.
"Let me introduce my brother to you," said Helene, her eyes shifting uneasily from Natasha to Anatole.

Natasha turned her pretty little head toward the elegant young officer and smiled at him over her bare shoulder. Anatole, who was just as handsome up close as from a distance, sat down beside her and told her he had long wanted this pleasure — ever since the Naryshkins' ball, in fact, at which he had had the well-remembered pleasure of seeing her. Kuragin was much more natural and at ease with women than among men. He talked boldly and freely, and Natasha was strangely and pleasantly struck by the fact that there was nothing intimidating about this man who was so much talked about, but that on the contrary his smile was completely open, cheerful, and good-natured.
Kuragin asked her opinion of the performance and told her how at a previous performance Semenova had fallen down on the stage.

"And do you know, Countess," he said, suddenly addressing her as an old familiar acquaintance, "we're organizing a costume tournament; you ought to take part in it! It will be great fun. We're all meeting at the Kargins'! Please come! No, really, eh?" said he.

While saying this he never took his smiling eyes off her face, her neck, and her bare arms. Natasha knew for certain that he was captivated by her. This pleased her, yet his presence made her feel constrained and uneasy. When she wasn't looking at him she felt that he was looking at her shoulders, and she involuntarily caught his eye so that he would look into her eyes rather than at her body. But looking into his eyes she was frightened, realizing that the barrier of modesty she had always felt between herself and other men didn't exist between them. She didn't know how it was that within five minutes she had come to feel terrifyingly close to this man. When she turned away she was afraid he might catch her from behind by her bare arm and kiss the back of her neck. They spoke of the most ordinary things, yet she felt that they were closer than she had ever been to any man. Natasha kept turning to Helene and to her father, as if asking what it all meant, but Helene was engaged in conversation with a general and didn't return her look, and her father's eyes said nothing but what they always said: "Having a good time? Well, I'm glad of it!"

During one of those moments of awkward silence when Anatole's prominent eyes were gazing calmly and steadily at her, Natasha, to break the silence, asked him how he liked Moscow. She asked the question and blushed. She felt the whole time that by talking to him she was doing something improper. Anatole smiled as though to encourage her.

"At first I didn't like it much, because what makes a city pleasant is the pretty women, isn't that so? But now I like it very much indeed," he said, looking at her meaningfully. "You'll come to the costume tournament, Countess? Do come!" and putting out his hand toward her bouquet and lowering his voice, he added, "You will be the prettiest there. Do come, dear countess, and give me this flower as a pledge!"
(The French phrase means: "Are the pretty women.")

Natasha didn't understand what he was saying any more than he did himself, but she felt that his incomprehensible words had an improper intention. She didn't know what to say and turned away as if she hadn't heard his remark. But as soon as she turned away she felt that he was there, behind her, so close behind her.

"How is he now? Confused? Angry? Should I set things right?" she asked herself, and she couldn't help turning around. She looked straight into his eyes, and his closeness, self-assurance, and the good-natured tenderness of his smile vanquished her. She smiled just as he was doing, gazing straight into his eyes. And again she felt with horror that no barrier existed between him and her.

The curtain rose again. Anatole left the box, calm and cheerful. Natasha went back to her father in the other box, now completely surrendered to the world she found herself in. Everything going on in front of her now seemed quite natural, but on the other hand all her previous thoughts of her fiance, of Princess Mary, or of life in the country didn't once enter her mind, as if they belonged to a remote past.

In the fourth act there was some kind of devil who sang while waving his arms about, till the boards were pulled out from under him and he disappeared below. That was the only part of the fourth act that Natasha saw. She felt agitated and tormented, and the cause of this was Kuragin, whom she couldn't help watching. As they were leaving the theater, Anatole came up to them, called their carriage, and helped them in. As he was handing Natasha in, he pressed her arm above the elbow. Agitated and flushed, she turned around. He was looking at her with glittering eyes, smiling tenderly.

Only after she had reached home was Natasha able to think clearly about what had happened to her, and suddenly remembering Prince Andrew she was horrified. At tea, to which everyone had sat down after the opera, she gave a loud cry, flushed, and ran out of the room.

"O God! I am lost!" she said to herself. "How could I let him?" She sat for a long time hiding her flushed face in her hands, trying to understand what had happened to her, but was unable either to grasp what had happened or what she felt. Everything seemed dark, confused, and terrible. There in that enormous, illuminated theater where the bare-legged Duport in a tinsel-decorated jacket jumped about to the music on wet boards, and young girls and old men, and the nearly naked Helene with her proud, calm smile, rapturously cried "bravo!" — there in the presence of that Helene it had all seemed clear and simple; but now, alone by herself, it was incomprehensible. "What is it? What was that terror I felt of him? What is this gnawing of conscience I'm feeling now?" she thought.

Only to the old countess at night in bed could Natasha have told all she was feeling. She knew that Sonya with her severe and simple views would either not understand it at all or be horrified at such a confession. So Natasha tried to work out what was tormenting her on her own.

"Am I ruined for Andrew's love or not?" she asked herself, and with comforting irony replied: "What a fool I am to ask that! What did happen to me? Nothing! I did nothing, I didn't lead him on at all. Nobody will know and I'll never see him again," she told herself. "So it's clear that nothing has happened and there's nothing to regret, and Andrew can love me still. But why 'still?' O God, why isn't he here?" Natasha calmed herself for a moment, but again some instinct told her that though all this was true, and though nothing had happened, yet the former purity of her love for Prince Andrew had been destroyed. And again in her imagination she went over her whole conversation with Kuragin, and again saw the face, gestures, and tender smile of that bold, handsome man when he pressed her arm.
